1 The shape of real reaction times

Part 6 left us with a Gaussian-distributed RT that is symmetric and bell-shaped. Real reaction times are not like that. They are right-skewed: there is a hard physical lower bound (motor response cannot be faster than ~150-200 ms) and a long tail of slow trials.

A common way to model right-skewed positive data is the log-normal distribution: if \(\log(\text{RT})\) is normally distributed, then RT itself is log-normal and strictly positive.

This part of the course:

  • Compares Gaussian and log-normal models on real LDT data.
  • Builds a generator that produces log-normal RTs.
  • Discusses how to back-transform effects from the log scale to the millisecond scale.
  • Runs a power analysis and a Type-I error check.

2 Real LDT data

Load a real LDT dataset (the same one used in Filip’s PhD work):

library(rio)
dat <- import("../data/raw_data/ldt_data.csv")
head(dat)
  subject ACC  RT stimuli syl_freq wrd_freq syl_freq.cod wrd_freq.cod
1    S001   0 680  jardin        b        a         -0.5         -0.5
2    S001   0 808   fusil        b        b         -0.5          0.5
3    S001   0 771   sonda        b        b         -0.5          0.5
4    S001   0 772    goma        b        a         -0.5         -0.5
5    S001   0 833   gorra        b        a         -0.5         -0.5
6    S001   0 700    dedo        a        a          0.5         -0.5

The dataset has one row per trial, with columns for subject, stimulus, condition (wrd_freq.cod), and RT in milliseconds.

3 Fitting the model: Gaussian vs log-normal

We compare two models on the same data: one assumes RT is normally distributed, the other models \(\log(\text{RT})\). Click between the tabs to compare the model output and the diagnostic panels.

  • Gaussian (raw RT)
  • Log-normal (log(RT))
m <- lmer(RT ~ wrd_freq.cod + (1 + wrd_freq.cod | subject) + (1 | stimuli),
          data = dat)
summary(m)

performance::check_model() produces a diagnostic panel for the model assumptions:

performance::check_model(m)

The QQ plot of residuals shows strong departure from normality in the upper tail, and the residuals-vs-fitted plot shows heteroscedasticity (the variance increases with the fitted value). Both are typical signatures of right-skewed data.

m_log <- lmer(log(RT) ~ wrd_freq.cod + (1 + wrd_freq.cod | subject) + (1 | stimuli),
              data = dat)
summary(m_log)

Same diagnostic panel for the log-transformed model:

performance::check_model(m_log)

The QQ plot is now much closer to the diagonal and the residual variance is more uniform. This is a substantial improvement.

The log-normal model wins on both diagnostic criteria. From here on the course commits to modelling \(\log(\text{RT})\) and the simulation generator switches from rnorm() to rlnorm().

4 Back to the millisecond scale

Fitting on the log scale costs us interpretability: the coefficients are no longer in milliseconds. To recover ms-scale effects we back-transform with exp().

With the fitted coefficients \(b_0 = 6.59\), \(b_1 = 0.10\) and \(\text{SE}(b_1) = 0.02\):

Show code (back-transform + 95% CI) 
b0        <- 6.59
b1        <- 0.10
b1_stderr <- 0.02

# point estimate
rt_high <- exp(b0 + b1 * -0.5)
rt_low  <- exp(b0 + b1 *  0.5)
effect  <- rt_low - rt_high

# 95% CI on b1 (log scale), then back-transform
lower <- b1 - 1.96 * b1_stderr
upper <- b1 + 1.96 * b1_stderr

effect_lower <- exp(b0 + lower * 0.5) - exp(b0 + lower * -0.5)
effect_upper <- exp(b0 + upper * 0.5) - exp(b0 + upper * -0.5)

c(rt_high      = rt_high,
  rt_low       = rt_low,
  effect_ms    = effect,
  effect_lower = effect_lower,
  effect_upper = effect_upper)
     rt_high       rt_low    effect_ms effect_lower effect_upper 
   692.28658    765.09499     72.80841     44.25589    101.38891

Two takeaways:

  • The point estimate is a ~70 ms effect, but this is conditional on the baseline RT being around 730 ms. The same log-scale effect (\(b_1 = 0.10\)) implies a different ms-scale effect at different baselines. This is the most important practical consequence of log-scale modelling.
  • The 95% CI on the ms scale spans roughly 40 to 100 ms — substantial uncertainty, worth keeping in mind when interpreting the point estimate.
Tip

In Bayesian terms, \(b_1 \sim \text{Normal}(0.10, 0.02)\). The back-transformed range above corresponds to a 95% credible interval on the ms-scale effect.

5 Generating log-normal RTs

To run a power analysis on this model, we need a data generator that produces log-normal RTs. The only changes from Part 6’s gendat_ldt_crossed():

  • All parameters are now on the log scale (so smaller numbers).
  • rnorm() becomes rlnorm() inside the row-by-row loop.
gendat_ldt_crossed_log <- function(n        = 20,    # subjects
                                   k        = 20,    # items per condition
                                   b0       = 6.59,  # log(grand mean RT); exp(6.59) ~ 730 ms
                                   b1       = 0.10,  # log-scale frequency effect (~70 ms on RT scale)
                                   sigma_u0 = 0.2,   # SD of subject intercepts (log)
                                   sigma_u1 = 0.02,  # SD of subject slopes (log)
                                   rho      = -0.5,  # correlation between subject intercepts and slopes
                                   sigma_w  = 0.1,   # SD of item intercepts (log)
                                   sigma    = 0.25) {# residual SD (log)

  # fully crossed design
  sim_dat          <- expand.grid(item = 1:(k * 2), subj = 1:n)
  sim_dat$cond.cod <- rep(c(-0.5, 0.5), each = k)

  # subject random effects (correlated intercepts and slopes)
  Sigma_u <- matrix(c(sigma_u0^2,                  rho * sigma_u0 * sigma_u1,
                      rho * sigma_u0 * sigma_u1,   sigma_u1^2),
                    nrow = 2)
  u <- mvrnorm(n     = length(unique(sim_dat$subj)),
               mu    = c(0, 0),
               Sigma = Sigma_u)

  # item random effects (intercepts only)
  w <- rnorm(n = length(unique(sim_dat$item)), mean = 0, sd = sigma_w)

  # generate RTs row by row -- note rlnorm() instead of rnorm()
  N  <- dim(sim_dat)[1]
  rt <- rep(NA, N)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    rt[i] <- rlnorm(1,
                    b0 +
                    u[sim_dat[i, ]$subj, 1] +
                    w[sim_dat[i, ]$item] +
                    (b1 + u[sim_dat[i, ]$subj, 2]) * sim_dat[i, ]$cond.cod,
                    sigma)
  }

  sim_dat$rt   <- rt
  sim_dat$subj <- factor(sim_dat$subj)
  sim_dat$item <- factor(sim_dat$item)
  sim_dat
}

Check that the resulting distribution is right-skewed:

sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = 100, k = 100)
hist(sim_dat$rt,
     main = "Distribution of Simulated RTs (Log-Normal)",
     xlab = "RT (ms)", col = "lightblue", breaks = 50)

Compare with the Gaussian histogram from Part 6 — the log-normal version has the characteristic right tail and a hard zero lower bound.

6 Sanity check on the log-normal model

Fit the same log(rt) model on simulated data to confirm the generator and the model agree:

sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = 20, k = 20)

m <- lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), sim_dat,
          control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
summary(m)

The fixed-effect estimates should be close to the generating values (6.59 and 0.10).

7 Power analysis

With the log-normal generator in hand, the power loop is identical in shape to the previous parts — only the simulator and model formula change:

nsim  <- 1000
pvals <- rep(NA, nsim)

for (i in 1:nsim) {
  sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = 20, k = 20,
                                    b0 = 6.59, b1 = 0.10,
                                    sigma_u0 = 0.2, sigma_u1 = 0.02,
                                    rho = -0.5, sigma_w = 0.1, sigma = 0.25)

  m <- lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), sim_dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
  pvals[i] <- summary(m)$coefficients[2, 5]
}

power <- round(mean(pvals < 0.05), digits = 4)
power
[1] 0.751

8 Parameter recovery (seven parameters now)

With the addition of \(\sigma_w\) and \(\rho\) on top of the standard four parameters, we now have seven parameters to recover:

nsim   <- 1000
params <- matrix(rep(NA, nsim * 7), ncol = 7)

for (i in 1:nsim) {
  sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = 20, k = 20,
                                    b0 = 6.59, b1 = 0.10,
                                    sigma_u0 = 0.2, sigma_u1 = 0.02,
                                    rho = -0.5, sigma_w = 0.1, sigma = 0.25)
  m <- lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), sim_dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

  params[i, 1] <- summary(m)$coefficients[1, 1] # b0
  params[i, 2] <- summary(m)$coefficients[2, 1] # b1
  params[i, 3] <- attr(VarCorr(m), "sc")        # residual SD
  vc           <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m))
  params[i, 4] <- vc$sdcor[1]                   # SD item intercepts
  params[i, 5] <- vc$sdcor[2]                   # SD subject slopes
  params[i, 6] <- vc$sdcor[3]                   # SD subject intercepts
  params[i, 7] <- vc$sdcor[4]                   # rho (subj intercept-slope correlation)
}

The fixed effects and large variance components recover cleanly. The correlation \(\rho\) is still the noisiest parameter, as we saw in Part 5.

9 Type-I error check

A useful sanity check on any new generative process: when the true effect is zero, what proportion of simulations falsely declare significance? The answer should be approximately \(\alpha = 0.05\).

nsim  <- 1000
pvals <- rep(NA, nsim)

for (i in 1:nsim) {
  sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = 20, k = 20,
                                    b0 = 6.59, b1 = 0,         # NO EFFECT
                                    sigma_u0 = 0.2, sigma_u1 = 0.0, # no slope variability
                                    rho = 0.0, sigma_w = 0.1, sigma = 0.25)

  m <- lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), sim_dat,
            control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
  pvals[i] <- summary(m)$coefficients[2, 5]
}

type1_error <- mean(pvals < 0.05)
type1_error
[1] 0.046

If the value is close to 0.05, the model and the generative process are consistent. Substantially higher would suggest the inference is anti- conservative; substantially lower, the model is conservative.

10 Summary and next step

In this part we:

  • Recognised that real RTs are right-skewed and not well-described by a Gaussian.
  • Fit log(RT) instead of RT to obtain better-behaved residuals.
  • Walked through the back-transformation from log(ms) to ms and showed that the ms-scale effect depends on the baseline RT.
  • Built gendat_ldt_crossed_log() to simulate from a log-normal generative process.
  • Verified power, parameter recovery, and the Type-I error rate.
Tip

For an interactive comparison of RT distributions (log-normal, ex-Gaussian, shifted log-normal, etc.), see Jonas K. Lindeløv’s shiny app.

The final form of the data-generating process is:

\[ \log(rt_{ij}) = \beta_0 + u_{0i} + w_{0j} + (\beta_1 + u_{1i}) \times \text{cond.cod}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij} \]

The next (final) part of the course iterates the power analysis across a grid of sample sizes and effect sizes, with confidence intervals on each estimate. This is the standard deliverable for a sample-size justification in a research proposal or pre-registration.
